title: Lean Ethereum
intro: In November 2024 Justin Drake proposed redoing Ethereum's consensus layer from a clean slate, first called the beam chain. By 2025 the name had widened to lean Ethereum, with the same idea applied to data and execution too. This is how it was argued: why start over, the worry that it should not arrive as one big upgrade, the tension between the lean research branch and the rest of protocol work, the hard parts of post-quantum signatures, and the Devcon 8 pull-forward. It is a proposal and a plan, not a scheduled upgrade.

stops.author: Roberto Saltini
stops.note: An early fast-finality design, a week before Devcon 7: finalise in about three slots rather than one, so slots can stay short. Posted by Roberto Saltini; the post lists Francesco D'Amato, Roberto Saltini, Thanh-Hai Tran and Luca Zanolini as its authors.

lines.text: As a result, our protocol achieves a shorter expected confirmation time compared to the previously proposed protocol, at the expense of a slight delay in block finalization, which extends to the time required to propose three additional blocks, rather than finalizing before the next block proposal.

Also, slot time is a crucial parameter affecting economic leakage in on-chain automated market makers (AMMs) due to arbitrage. Specifically, arbitrage profits -- and consequently, liquidity providers’ (LP) losses -- are proportional to the square root of slot time. Therefore, reducing slot time is highly desirable for financial applications on smart contract blockchains.

stops.author: vbuterin
stops.source_title: Long-term L1 execution layer proposal: replace the EVM with RISC-V
stops.note: Lean execution begins as a written proposal: the same ambition for the execution layer as the beam chain has for the consensus layer.

lines.text: This post proposes a radical idea for the future of the Ethereum execution layer, one that is equally as ambitious as the beam chain effort is for the consensus layer. It aims to greatly improve the efficiency of the Ethereum execution layer, resolving one of the primary scaling bottlenecks, and can also greatly improve the execution layer's simplicity - in fact, it is perhaps the only way to do so.
The idea: replace the EVM with RISC-V as the virtual machine language that smart contracts are written in.

stops.author: levs57
stops.source_title: Long-term L1 execution layer proposal: replace the EVM with RISC-V
stops.note: The sharpest substantive reply in the first hours of the RISC-V thread: precompiles stay, so the simplicity gain is smaller than hoped, and RISC-V may not be the right instruction set.

lines.text: Therefore, any change to cryptographic primitives of the base layer will require writing and auditing circuits for these precompiles. This is a severe restriction.

My recommendation is, instead, constructing a proof-friendly architecture with minimal MMU allowing to run contracts as separate executables; I don't think it should be RISC-V; rather a separate ISA - ideally, aware of limitations dictated by SNARK protocols.

stops.author: Justin Drake
stops.note: The proposer's own written definition: the beam chain becomes lean consensus, and the idea widens to data and execution. He also names the diversity of views as welcome.

lines.text:
lean consensus is beacon chain 2.0: hardened for ultimate security and decentralization, plus finality in seconds; formerly branded as "beam chain"
lean data is blobs 2.0: post-quantum blobs, plus granular blob sizing for a calldata-like developer experience
lean execution is EVM 2.0: a minimal, SNARK-friendly instruction set (possibly RISC-V; pronounced "risk five"), boosting performance while preserving EVM compatibility and its network effects
A healthy diversity of views across Protocol, the EF, and the broader Ethereum community is expected and welcome. It strengthens us.

stops.author: Ed Felten
stops.source_title: Why RISC-V Is Not a Good Choice for an L1 Delivery ISA, and Why WASM Is a Better One
stops.note: A reasoned alternative to RISC-V for lean execution. The post says it expresses the view of Offchain Labs and names four authors (Mario Alvarez, Matteo Campanelli, Tsahi Zidenberg, Daniel Lumi); it was posted by the Ed Felten account.

lines.text: We support these goals but question Vitalik’s implicit assumption that one ISA can optimally serve both ZK-proving and smart contract delivery. Since enshrining an ISA on L1 primarily affects how smart contracts are delivered to the chain, we should evaluate ISAs based on their suitability for general delivery and storage on chain, not proving alone.

RISC-V, as an open standard for hardware, is an impressive and influential technology. RISC-V was designed for simplicity and ease of implementation in hardware. However, there is no reason to expect that RISC-V-based ZK-VMs will be the ultimate arrival point of the evolution of ZK-VMs; more likely, they are just one step along the way.

stops.note: The Strawmap, the document most later stops refer to, published as strawmap.org on 25 Feb 2026 (site source github.com/ethereum/strawmap: first commit 23 Feb, FAQ finalised 25 Feb; the page itself carries no date). Started as an EF workshop discussion starter in Jan 2026 (the page says so). Author line on the page: 'by EF protocol', 'maintained by EF Architecture'.

lines.text: The strawman roadmap originated as a discussion starter at an EF workshop in Jan 2026, with the aim of helping integrate lean Ethereum with shorter-term initiatives.

It acknowledges the limits of drafting a roadmap in a highly decentralized ecosystem. An “official” roadmap reflecting all Ethereum stakeholders is effectively impossible. Rough consensus is fundamentally an emergent, continuous, and inherent uncertain process.

stops.note: A pace objection from inside the discussion: register something already trusted now and choose the post-quantum scheme later, once it is vetted.

lines.text: Why not just then register hashed BLS keys instead? BLS keys are already part of the operator's workflow and are safe as long as they haven't signed anything. We could just keep them and sign with them the move to PQ only after the PQ system has been fully chosen and vetted.

stops.source_title: Exploring the Design Space for a Post-Quantum Public Key Registry for Ethereum Validators
stops.note: The reply to the hashed-BLS-keys idea: a quantum computer can recover BLS private keys from public ones, so those keys cannot be treated as secret.

lines.text:
Not sure what you mean by this but remember that a CRQP can recover private BLS keys from the public ones. 

If you're proposing to record hashed public BLS keys then you're effectively treating public BLS keys as secret keys and requiring that their owners don't sign anything, which is pretty much impossible given that BLS pairs are used in the consensus algorithm.

stops.author: Thomas Coratger
stops.source_title: Exploring the Design Space for a Post-Quantum Public Key Registry for Ethereum Validators
stops.note: The authors' answer: the design is open, and even the signature scheme is not final. Posted by Thomas Coratger, whose post lists five authors.

lines.text: As indicated throughout the post and in the open questions, all these topics remain widely open for alternative designs.

Technically speaking, even the signature scheme itself is not 100% confirmed because if someone comes up with a magical PQ signature scheme with much better aggregation properties, this is certainly something we have to consider.

stops.author: OisinKyne
stops.note: The decentralisation worry about the lean consensus direction, in a reply to Vitalik's 'extremely lean chain' post: a small minority controlling the chain, and the loss of staking in groups.

lines.text: Do you think this design might hide centralisation more than it enables decentralisation? Imo it hides centralisation by way of key rotation, withdrawal credential hiding, etc. It doesn't really enable decentralisation (other than maybe taking pseudonymity to anonymity).

A particular concern of mine is that so far Lean intends to drop the ability to stake in groups. This has been a design goal since ~2018 for the chain, and not one that we should silently drop. Would you be willing to explain why its no longer a design goal, or to commit to working on an architecture until we can keep it?

stops.author: vbuterin
stops.note: Vitalik says he is personally strongly in favor of group staking continuing to be a goal, and names the privacy trade-off as real.

lines.text: I'm personally strongly in favor of this continuing to be a goal.

Doesn't anything privacy-related enable hiding centralization? eg. even including private payments, or private voting. I feel like it's a genuine issue but a bullet that we have to bite if we are pro-privacy at all.

stops.speaker: Justin Drake
stops.note: A hard part of the post-quantum plan, in the proposer's words: signature schemes cannot be changed once launched, while the proving machine can be upgraded at every fork. Solo talk, single credited speaker.

lines.clean: For the signature schemes in particular, once we've launched them, there's no going back. Most likely they will be extremely sticky, and the designs that we launch with will persist for many years to come, but possibly decades or centuries. On the other hand, [leanVM], it's okay if it's not perfect, because it's infrastructure that's hidden behind the scenes that we can upgrade at every hard fork.

stops.speaker: Justin Drake
stops.note: How the idea moved, in the proposer's words, answering an audience question: post-quantum was once the excuse for a bigger revamp; with quantum timelines earlier it is now taken on its own. Q&A with a moderator; the answers are Justin Drake's.

lines.clean: Two years ago, I gave a presentation at [Devcon] on the beam chain, and the idea back then was to use post-quantum as a [Schelling] point for doing an ambitious revamp of the whole consensus layer. The argument back then was that if we're going to do a very invasive change like post-quantum, we might as well also do all the other things that we've been wanting to do, for example have a much better finality mechanism and clean up all the technical debt. You can think of it as being proof of stake 2.0. In some sense what I'm saying today, two years later, is the exact opposite.

stops.title: A plan, not a scheduled upgrade
stops.body: According to the EF Protocol post of 7 September 2026, fast-finality research now decouples finality from block production, with decoupled consensus the leading headliner candidate for I*. The post sets December 2029 as the target for a quantum-resistant L1 across all three layers, a deadline it calls non-negotiable at least until January 2027, and says the Strawmap may swap K* and L*, moving lean consensus forward by one fork. The Strawmap drawing on strawmap.org is now dated 2 November 2026: it places post-quantum transactions in the fork called I*, post-quantum attestations and post-quantum data sampling in J*, and the post-quantum L1 goal in J*, matching the update Justin Drake announced at Devcon 8 on 3 November. Earlier versions (July, 19 August) put full post-quantum readiness later.
stops.note: Primary sources: EF Protocol, Current and Emerging Priorities, blog.ethereum.org/2026/09/07/protocol-priorities (December 2029 target, 'non-negotiable at least until January 2027', the possible K*/L* swap); strawmap.org (EF Architecture, seven forks by 2029, timelines are a guide; Glamsterdam and Hegota are the named forks, later ones placeholders). Status read on 4 Nov 2026. strawmap.org drawing read 10 Nov 2026, 'updated Nov 2, 2026' (I*: leanSPHINCS post-quantum transactions, decoupled consensus; J*: leanXMSS post-quantum attestations, leanDA sampling, post-quantum L1 north star). This matches the Devcon 8 update of 3 Nov 2026 (stop s-14). Press says Drake called December 2028 an aspiration at Devcon 8; that is not an official change and the body does not state it.

excluded.reason: Thomas Coratger, Post-Quantum Interop Call #49, 29 Jul 2026 (confirmed speaker; drafted as stop s-13, then cut after the independent check): a devnet testing note with unexplained jargon (sub-MTU XMSS, the main LeanVM branch) that repeats the signature-size point Gajinder Singh makes at EthCC[9]. Stop id s-13 is left unused so other ids stay stable.

Unchained, 25 Mar 2025 (Alex Stokes and Barnabe Monnot, both credited, no per-speaker labels): one guest says the beam chain is 'a very nice thought experiment' and 'a terminal vision', the other that 'it's not enough to have great designs for 2029, you also need to beef up what you currently have'. The best objection by people who are not Drake, but which of the two speaks each turn cannot be confirmed from the captions.

Ethereum Korea One clients panel, 29 Sep 2026, ord 35 to 38: a panelist prefers reusing BLS for transient post-quantum safety (the Offchain Labs paper) over replacing it with hash-based signatures. A real alternative to the lean approach, but the four panelists are credited without labels and the speaker of that turn (not Luca Zanolini) is not confirmed.

Post-Quantum Interop Call #29, Benedikt Wagner, ord 65 (confirmed speaker): with SNARKs one can aggregate signatures over different messages if the relation proven in leanVM is designed right. Replying to a spec question, it does not stand alone as a reason why aggregation is hard. Gajinder Singh's #36 ord 28 to 29 is about not testing fork mechanisms in devnets yet, not signatures.

Zero Knowledge Ep. 394, ord 43 to 44: the trade-offs between XMSS aggregated per second, recursion time and network cost of exchanging post-quantum objects. Thomas Coratger and Emil are both credited and the transcript has no speaker labels, so the voice is not confirmed.

Justin Drake, Zero Knowledge Ep. 391, ord 9 to 10 (drafted, then replaced): post-quantum signatures about ten times larger than BLS. Replaced by Gajinder Singh's EthCC[9] lines to reduce Drake's share. The Bankless 23 Mar 2026 rewrite-is-already-needed stop was also cut because the 'rewrites never work' answer carries the same point.

Anthony Sassano, The Daily Gwei 19 Nov 2024, ord 36 to 45 (confirmed, drafted, then cut for length): argues the timeline slide was Justin Drake's biggest mistake and that recruiting new client teams makes sense. A commentator, and the map is capped at 18 stops.

Vitalik Buterin, EDCON 2025, ord 42 to 43 (confirmed, drafted, then cut for length): 'lean Ethereum will be Ethereum 3.0', every piece simple, secure, optimal. Overlaps Justin Drake's definition on Bankless, and set beside the Programmable Cryptography stop (Vitalik: 'Can we call beam chain Ethereum 3.0? I think no') it would read as a gotcha. Do not bring back.

Georgios Konstantopoulos (Reth), Devcon 7 Q&A: asked whether Reth should build a beam chain client he answers 'not many' thoughts, then 'I don't know', 'we maintain so much code'. A candid capacity remark, not a position on the redesign, and the flat tone reads as a gotcha. Not used.

Devcon 7 Infinite Endgames panel (only Lightclient credited, several voices): the best sceptical lines on the map's theme (fossil before the beam chain, 'people will say too complex, let's do it during the beam chain', 'we're not going to ship the beam chain if we're not equally confident', 'at the moment it's nothing, it's just an idea', ords 78 to 82). Voices change without handover cues, so the speaker of each turn cannot be confirmed.

leanConsensus Calls #1 to #5 and #7 (e.g. cfcc0382, d15df1b0, 21794f94, 5b336755, f3efb71b, 97ae8278), the Beam Day talks at EthCC[8] (e.g. 25e27ecf, 28d408a9, 2a9c66f8, 8587c115), Native Rollups Calls and the 2025 Post-Quantum Interop Calls #1 to #18: auto-captions with no speaker labels and no credited speaker, so no voice can be confirmed. Only call #6 (labelled) is quoted.

No confirmed client-team voice sceptical of a rewrite, its timeline or its distraction from nearer work was found, despite searches for misheard forms (beam chain, bean chain, lean consensus with each client name, rewrite, ossification, from scratch). The doubts on the map come from Dankrad Feist, Vitalik Buterin and Tomasz Stanczak. ACD calls #158, #187 and ACDE #238 mention leanVM or the lookahead only in passing.

Bankless 15 Nov 2024, Unchained recaps (eb9294f6, d22f5e05) and Chopping Block shows (6cf0875a, 5ec8fc7d, e468378c): hosts and guests describing the hostile reaction ('big refactoring', 'we may reach Mars before beam chain goes live') or the shifting names (beam chain, strawmap). Second-hand reporting and characterisations of named people, not used. Haseeb Qureshi (3e2d1606) calls the beam chain a concession that the rollup-centric roadmap was a mistake: a commentator's take, not used.

Guillaume Ballet (Geth), Devcon 7 verkle talk, ord 19 to 20: says the beam chain shows the end game keeps changing and warns of two transitions instead of one. It is about verkle versus binary trees, not about the consensus redesign, so left out.

Justin Drake, EthCC[9] Staking Strawmap, ord 33 to 36: finishing the post-quantum migration by 2029, ten client teams and four devnets. Confirmed speaker, left out to avoid repeating points already made by Justin's Bankless stops and Gajinder Singh's.

P2P Networking Call #6, Kamil Salakhiev, ord 122 to 148: lean data (replacing KZG with Merkle commitments plus a leanVM proof of 128 to 512 kilobytes). Confirmed speaker but the captions are too garbled to clean without guessing.

All Core Devs - Execution #238, Mo Jahanara, ord 140: private withdrawals are 'very unlikely' for Hegota because leanVM must be mature and audited. About a privacy proposal, not the lean consensus argument.

Post-Quantum Interop Calls #28 to #49 (labelled speakers): many confirmed status updates (Benedikt Wagner on aggregating different messages in #29 ord 65, Gajinder Singh on not adding forks to devnets yet in #36 ord 28 to 29, Thomas Coratger on DevNets). None of #28 to #49 is quoted (#49 is x-coratger-49); they are progress logs that repeat the same point.

leanConsensus Call #6: 3-slot finality (16 May 2025; Francesco D'Amato, Luca Zanolini, Vitalik Buterin and Roberto Saltini, labelled speakers): presents 3SF and Vitalik's 3SF-mini prototype. Redundant with the 3SF post (stop w-3sf-2024), which says the same more clearly.

Ethproofs Call #4: Enshrine RISC-V? (22 Aug 2025): the live debate on lean execution, but no credited speaker and no labels in the captions, so no voice can be confirmed. The written RISC-V stops (Vitalik, levs57, Offchain Labs) carry the argument.

Can Ethereum Compete with Bitcoin, Solana & Celestia? (9 Dec 2024, ord 128 to 132): the two credited hosts criticise the beam chain talk (no clear 'why', wrong priorities). Two voices without labels, so the speaker of each line cannot be confirmed.

What's the Best Way for Ethereum to Grow? Two Ethereans Debate (26 Nov 2024; Justin Drake and Martin Koppelmann, ord 73 to 78): Drake explains the clean-slate beam chain. Two voices without labels and he says the same on Bankless (stop s-05).

Vitalik Buterin, EDCON 2025 (The Next Five Years of Ethereum Core Technology), ord 42 to 44: lean Ethereum as the long-term future, with a quantum estimate. Confirmed speaker, left out for the same reason as x-vitalik-edcon (overlaps Justin Drake's definition and the Ethereum 3.0 line reads as a gotcha beside stop s-04).

Getting to Lean Ethereum (Devcon 8, 4 Nov 2026; Leandro Ferrigno and Ivan Litteri of LambdaClass): a client team explains that lean features no longer ship as one hard fork and the old and new roadmaps are meeting. Two credited speakers with a handover that the captions do not label, so the speaker of each line is unconfirmed.
Federico Carrone, Next 10 Years of Ethereum (Devconnect 2025), ord 39: praise for lean Ethereum as 'a cathedral'. Supportive colour rather than an argument.

Ben Adams, An Ethereum Validator in Every Home (Devcon 8, 4 Nov 2026): a design talk for very light validators built on lean pieces (leanVM numbers, decoupled consensus). Not an argument about the lean plan itself.

Bankless 18 Nov 2024 (Justin Drake) and the Empire show of the same day (aa813c5c, three credited voices, no labels): the same beam chain pitch as the Devcon keynote and the 2 Dec 2024 Bankless interview already on the map.
GAP, no transcript: Long-term L1 Proposal: Replacing the EVM with RISC-V (Vitalik Buterin, 13 Jun 2025). His written proposal is on the map instead (w-vbuterin-riscv-2025).
GAP, no transcript: 'Lean Ethereum' (4 May 2026).

GAP, no transcript: Ethereum's Future: The Strawmap, Glamsterdam & Hegota (Parithosh Jayanthi, Berlin Ethereum Day, 15 Jun 2026). A draft of the same title, 'From strawmap to reality' (92bf2e9b), is unpublished and has no transcript.
GAP, unpublished draft with no transcript: Fast Finality, Faster blocks (Francesco, January 2026). The published Devconnect 2025 version is on the map (s-15).
GAP, no transcript: Introduction to hash-based proof systems (Diego Kingston, Devcon 7).

Written candidates read and left out as minor or redundant: Justin Drake's reply on beam chain client teams and proof sizes (ethresear.ch/t/21027/2), benaadams on 256-bit arithmetic (Magicians 23617/2), gcolvin on replacing the EVM (ethresear.ch/t/23491/17), Luca Zanolini on dynamic availability and the replies (ethresear.ch/t/24418), Vitalik Buterin's opening post of 'The Extremely Lean Chain' (ethresear.ch/t/25369/1), the 3SF and registry posts' remaining paragraphs, and Pardis Toolabi's lattice-or-hash guide (ethresear.ch/t/26003), a field guide rather than a position.

spec_changes.change: Lean Ethereum unveiled by Justin Drake on the EF blog: three layers (lean consensus = beacon chain 2.0, formerly beam chain; lean data; lean execution) and hash-based cryptography as the common thread. Not an EIP; the roadmap's own milestone.
spec_changes.agreed_at: No call; a personal vision post that states a diversity of views across Protocol is expected

spec_changes.change: Strawmap published at strawmap.org (seven forks through 2029, five north stars; originated at an EF workshop in January 2026). Date from the ethereum/strawmap commits (first 23 Feb, FAQ final 25 Feb) and press.
Strawmap update adds the MV-PQ milestone at J*; superseded by the Strawmap drawing dated 2 Nov 2026, which s-status now describes.
EF Protocol priorities: Dec 2029 quantum-resistant L1 target, possible K*/L* swap, Hegota has little appetite for more consensus scope.
pq-devnet-0 to pq-devnet-4 milestones on leanroadmap.org (leanroadmap.org page read May 2026 version).
spec_changes.why_not: Progress log, no argument or decision.

spec_changes.change: Strawmap drawing updated 2 Nov 2026 (post-quantum items in J*), announced by Justin Drake at Devcon 8 on 3 Nov.
